### Insertion of non-viral domains

Another rational design approach is incorporation of exogenous sequence into the capsid. For example, in an effort to enhance BBB transport, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) were incorporated into AAV9-derived capsids to yield variants such as AAV.CPP.16 (Table 1), which demonstrated up to 249-fold enhanced transduction efficiency in the murine brain. Of the transduced cells, approximately 80% were neurons, 15% astrocytes, and 1% oligodendrocytes. Furthermore, depending on brain region, this variant showed a 2.0- to 8.6-fold increase in transduction efficiency when administered intravenously to adult NHPs. By enhancing transcytosis and cellular uptake, this vector effectively mediated transgene delivery, including in models of glioblastoma.24

Recent studies have demonstrated that inserting nanobody domains into structurally permissive capsid regions, such as the 2/5-fold wall and the 5-fold pore, can confer receptor-specific targeting without compromising viral infectivity.25 For instance, introduction of a fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-specific nanobody into AAV capsids enabled selective transduction of FAP-expressing cells, with the most effective variant demonstrating up to an 18-fold increase in the ratio of target to off-target infection compared with unmodified AAV in vitro.25 Moreover, guided by structural accessibility and capsid stability, eight different insertion points on the AAV capsid surface were tested. Positions in the 2-fold valley (Q259, N262, and Q387), protruding 5-fold pore (N328, N337), depression around the pore (N554, S670), and the previously validated T456 at the 3-fold protrusion were chosen based on their ability to accommodate insertions without compromising capsid integrity. Modifications at positions such as N262 and T456 resulted in up to an 8-fold enhancement in transduction efficiency in FAP-positive cells (Table 1).

### Bioconjugation for targeting and immune evasion

Bioconjugation has been another approach being pursued to address immune responses and targeting specificity. Lee et al. investigated the potential of polyethylene glycol (PEG) conjugation to enhance the immune evasion of AAV vectors by reducing neutralization from pre-existing antibodies.26 The authors systematically evaluated the effect of PEG molecular weight and conjugation ratio on viral infectivity and immune protection, and the resulting modified AAV exhibited a modest 2.3-fold improvement in resistance to antibody neutralization in vitro compared with unmodified vectors. However, exceeding this conjugation threshold led to a marked decline in infectivity, likely due to steric hindrance affecting critical viral interactions (Table 1).

Bioconjugation can also be used to change the tropism of an AAV capsid. For example, attaching N-acetylgalactosamine ligands to AAV2 capsids enhanced hepatocyte targeting in primary mouse hepatocytes by 2.4- to 5.6-fold while reducing interactions with neutralizing antibodies in vitro by 4-fold compared with AAV2 (Table 1).27 However, a general challenge for bioconjugation is the complexity of manufacturing, as additional production steps may reduce yields and increase reproducibility risk.

## Directed evolution

Our incomplete understanding of AAV interactions with host tissues and cells can pose a significant limitation for rational design approaches, and high-throughput, unbiased discovery methods such as directed evolution offer complementary advantages in discovering enhanced vectors. Directed evolution emulates natural evolution by creating a diverse library of biomolecules and applying an iterative, functional selective pressure(s) to yield variants with desired properties,28 even when the molecular and biological mechanisms underlying the limitations of extant vectors are unknown.

In 2006 Maheshri et al.29 generated a diverse AAV2 capsid library using random point mutagenesis and recombination, followed by selective pressure to isolate variants with improved properties. Heparin-affinity chromatography was used to identify mutants with both higher and lower affinity receptor binding, resulting in altered tropism. Also, to address antibody neutralization, the AAV library was passed on cells in the presence of anti-AAV2 serum, leading to the identification of a variant with a 96-fold increase in antibody resistance compared with wild-type AAV2. In vivo testing confirmed that this variant retained gene delivery efficiency, even in the presence of high levels of neutralizing antibodies, demonstrating the clinical potential of this approach.

Researchers have generated other capsid libraries including random peptide insertions,17 loop swapping,18 and DNA shuffling.19 These libraries have enabled the identification of novel AAV variants with enhanced immune evasion, altered tropism, and enhanced transduction efficiency across various cell and tissue types. For example, in 2013, Dalkara et al.30 selected error-prone, shuffled, and peptide insertion libraries for the capacity to penetrate dense tissue in the retina and reach photoreceptors from the vitreous. Their resulting AAV2-based vector, 7m8, could infect photoreceptors after intravitreal injection in mice and, to a lesser extent, NHP30 (Table 1).

More recent studies have evolved AAV capsids with improved muscle tropism and immune evasion properties. For instance, Tabebordbar et al.31 inserted random 7-mer peptides between amino acids 588 and 589 of the hypervariable region VIII of the AAV9 capsid. Using a stringent in vivo RNA expression selection strategy, coupled with next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis, researchers performed two parallel rounds of selection in mice and NHPs. They prioritized capsid variants that effectively transduced skeletal muscle while minimizing off-target accumulation in the liver. This approach led to the identification of MyoAAV 1A, an engineered capsid containing an RGD motif that exhibited 10–29 times greater muscle transduction compared with AAV9 in mice, as well as enhanced gene delivery to cardiac tissue. Further evolution through mutagenesis of the peptide flanking residues resulted in MyoAAV 2A (Table 1), a second-generation variant with an expanded affinity for multiple integrin heterodimers and up to 128-fold higher transduction efficiency in human myotubes compared with AAV9. These MyoAAV capsids also demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in Duchenne muscular dystrophy and X-linked myotubular myopathy mouse models, achieving functional recovery at 10- to 250-fold lower doses than conventional AAV9-based vectors.

There has also been progress in understanding the importance of choosing the model system for evolution. For example, capsids optimized in one species may not perform equivalently in others, necessitating the development of vectors specialized for one species or the use of multi-species selective pressures. The variants AAV-PHP.B and AAV-PHP.eB (Table 1) were evolved using a Cre-selection strategy for highly efficient BBB crossing and neuronal tropism in the mouse CNS,32 although they exhibited lower efficiency in NHPs. By comparison, AAV Cap.Mac (Table 1), which was evolved for BBB crossing in NHPs, showed increased transduction efficiency in the CNS of newborn macaques after intravenous (i.v.) injection and demonstrates neuronal and glial tropism in the CNS of mice after intracerebroventricular (although not i.v.) administration.33,34 These examples illustrate the general concept that evolution generates what is selected for. An alternative approach is to evolve across species to generate a single variant that can, for example, enable efficacy testing in mouse models and translatability to larger animal models. Rosales et al.20 exemplified this strategy to develop AAV variants with enhanced kidney tropism. Through iterative cycling in murine, porcine, and NHP kidney models, as well as human kidney organoids, they identified AAV.k13 and AAV.k20 (Table 1), which demonstrated up to 20,000-fold enrichment compared with AAV9 in human organoid cultures and 25,000- to 28,000-fold enrichment in ex vivo perfused NHP kidneys. Moreover, AAV.k13 and AAV.k20 exhibited approximately 3- to 9-fold higher selectivity over AAV9 respectively, therefore showing that these are promising vectors for gene therapy applications in kidney diseases and transplantation.

Additional efforts have utilized structural insights to enhance immune evasion. Notably, Havlik et al.35 blended structural analysis with an evolution strategy to engineer AAV capsids with both reduced antibody susceptibility and modified tropism. After mapping antigenic footprints on the AAV8 capsids via cryo-electron microscopy, they systematically introduced mutations in surfaced-exposed variable regions through saturation mutagenesis, followed by iterative selection in human hepatocyte cultures. This process led to the development of AAVhum.8 (Table 1), an AAV8 variant that exhibited a 10-fold increase in human hepatocyte transduction with a 2- to 6-fold reduction in antibody susceptibility compared with AAV8. The evolved variant incorporated mutations across four key antigenic regions, VR-IV, VR-V, VR-VIII, and the HI loop, each of which contributed to a refined capsid surface topology that reduced antibody binding without compromising capsid stability or manufacturability. Functional validation in a humanized liver mouse model further demonstrated that AAVhum.8 transduced 34.4% of human hepatocytes, a 10-fold improvement over AAV8.

### Computationally guided library design for evolution

SCHEMA36 is an algorithm that identifies the optimal recombination positions that minimize structural disruption in a family of proteins, and it was applied to create a recombination library using six natural AAV serotype sequences that have a potentially greater proportion of stably folding capsids compared with random, DNA shuffling-based recombination.34 This design resulted in a highly diversified chimeric capsid library with more than 1.6 million variants. They also used a stringent Cre-dependent in vivo selection strategy in mice to target neural stem cells (NSCs) in the subventricular zone. This approach led to the identification of a novel variant, SCH9 (Table 1), that exhibited a 24-fold greater transduction efficiency of NSCs and a 12-fold greater transduction volume than AAV9 in vivo. SCH9 was found to utilize both galactose and heparan sulfate as cell surface receptors. Additionally, it demonstrated increased resistance to neutralizing antibodies.

Santiago-Ortiz et al.37 applied phylogenetic reconstruction to generate the sequence of putative ancestral AAV capsids but allowed diversity at amino acid positions that could not be predicted with high certainty. Subjecting the resulting experimentally constructed library to iterative selection on a diverse cell line panel yielded broadly infectious variants with transduction efficiencies comparable with the most effective extant serotypes. These ancestral AAV variants exhibited increased thermostability and did not rely on sialic acid, galactose, or heparan sulfate proteoglycans for cellular entry, distinguishing them from natural serotypes. In vivo analysis further demonstrated that selected variants achieved 19- to 31-fold greater gene expression in murine muscle tissue compared with AAV1. In parallel efforts, Zinn et al.38 successfully engineered a novel AAV capsid, Anc80L65, using ancestral sequence reconstruction. Further characterization of this variant demonstrated high stability and transduction efficiency in mouse and NHP relative to AAV2 and AAV8, as well as higher thermal stability properties38 (Table 1).

### NGS-aided evolution

Early efforts in capsid engineering were limited by sequencing throughput and read length. The advent of short read NGS dramatically increased throughput of directed evolution screens39 This holds true especially for libraries such as random peptide insertions whose diversity is localized to small regions that can readily be sequenced. Korbelin et al. conducted an in vivo screen in mouse model where they used NGS to monitor the pool of capsid libraries during each step of the selection. This led to the discovery of a novel capsid with the ability to transduce endothelium and pulmonary vasculature 270-fold better than wild-type or other control capsid variants.40

The use of DNA barcodes was another notable advance for using NGS to analyze AAV libraries. By associating each mutant with a unique DNA barcode, this method allows for simultaneous phenotypic characterization of hundreds of AAV variants in a single experiment.39 The authors demonstrated the power of AAV Barcode-Seq by constructing a comprehensive AAV9 capsid mutant library in which 381 amino acids across the C-terminal half of the viral capsid were systematically mutated. Through multiplexed Illumina sequencing, they quantified how each mutation affected critical properties such as viral stability, receptor binding, tissue tropism, blood clearance, and immune evasion. They discovered mutants including AAV9 P504A/G505A and Q590A that exhibited a more than 200-fold decrease in murine liver transduction compared with AAV9.

Pekrun et al.,41 expanding on the role of DNA barcoding in directed evolution, identified AAV capsids, from two barcoded capsid-shuffled libraries, optimized for transduction of pancreatic β cells in human islets. The variant AAV-KP1, a chimeric capsid that combines sequences from different viral serotypes, exhibited up to 10-fold greater transduction efficiency compared with existing AAV vectors (Table 1).

While barcoding has thus been promising, barcode swapping, which results from genome recombination during packaging, can pose significant challenges for downstream variant identification. Recombination events leading to barcode chimerism are length and homology dependent and occur independently of capsid serotype.42 This can result in high rates of discordant barcode pairs, with long homologous inserts exhibiting swap rates exceeding 60%, potentially necessitating minimizing homology regions and optimizing packaging conditions.

Single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing, more commonly known as long read sequencing, has further expanded the capabilities of high-throughput sequencing in AAV directed evolution by enabling single read sequencing of the entire cap gene, enabling analysis of variants including chimeras or random point mutants whose diversity spans all of VP1.43 As of 2025, PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing is able to read up to 25 kb in length with approximately 6 million reads at an accuracy of 99.95%.44 By applying SMRT sequencing to human tissue samples, researchers successfully identified AAVv66, a novel capsid that differs by 13 amino acid substitutions relative to AAV2, predominantly in the VP3 regions that influence receptor binding and particle stability (Table 1). Functionally, AAVv66 exhibited a 2.4-fold packaging efficiency and approximately a 13-fold enhancement in CNS cell transduction in mice compared with AAV.

## ML

In recent years, ML or artificial intelligence has played an increasing role in AAV capsid engineering. ML relies on the computational identification of patterns in a dataset that can then be harnessed to engineer improved function or to test scientific hypotheses.52 ML-based algorithms primarily fall in two categories: supervised or unsupervised learning.53 The former uses labeled data, allowing the algorithm to establish a relationship between the input, i.e., the features that are fed to the model, and the output, i.e., the property the algorithm is intended to predict. By comparison, unsupervised learning allows the program to make its own discoveries within the data without such external guidance.

In the first application of ML to AAV capsids, Ógden et al. synthesized an AAV2 capsid library containing all single-codon substitutions, deletions, and insertions at each of the 735 amino acid positions. The library was subjected to phenotypic selection, including packaging fitness, thermostability, monoclonal antibody neutralization, and biodistribution. Sequencing the barcoded libraries before and after each selection yielded datasets linking sequence to enrichment, which were used to train ML algorithms to predict sequence-function relationships. The resulting algorithms were used to enable the design of an additional capsid library of 1,271 variants in addition to the 10,047 randomly generated mutants with increased tropism to the murine liver relative to wildtype.6 This trend was more prevalent with mutants with four or more mutations, whereas 4,477 of the randomly generated mutants demonstrated weaker liver tropism than wild type (99.8%). Additionally, during library diversification, the researchers found a novel open reading frame 3, membrane associated accessory protein (MAAP), which has subsequently been found to regulate viral release from cells.54

In subsequent work by the same group, Sinai et al. targeted an immunologically relevant, 28-amino-acid region (560–588) in the VP3 of AAV2 and demonstrated that a variational auto encoded can generate novel capsid sequences. The variational autoencoder, a type of unsupervised model generation, was trained on a 564-sample multiple sequence alignment of dependovirus data55 and complemented the dataset by incorporating 22,704 samples from a deep mutational exploration. As a result, their generative models were able to produce capsid mutants with more than 50% of the initial 28 amino acid positions substituted, and multiple variants that had substitutions in almost every position of this region that were deemed fit or viable. This had not been observed previously given that random amino acid mutations in the 560–588 region had been shown to ablate capsid particle viability. In other work, Huang et al.56 constructed a supervised variational auto-encoder that incorporates labeled data during the training of the model to improve the structure and interpretability of the predictive system. To engineer a capsid with increased infectivity in the CNS,56 they used a pull-down assay to screen for capsids that effectively bind in vitro to LY6A and LY6C1, proteins expressed on the murine BBB. Top candidate variants from the initial screen demonstrated increased transduction in the murine CNS, and the pull-down assay dataset was then used to train a predictive model that would generate additional functional sequences. Capsid sequences designed in silico demonstrated greater transduction efficiency relative to the top performers from the first round of screening.

Most protein mutations are deleterious to function, and accordingly it was found that the majority of AAV peptide insertion variants have lower packaging fitness than the parental wild type.57 Zhu et al.58 applied ML to enhance the packaging fitness of a peptide insertion library and thereby potentially increase the number of high-quality variants emerging for a subsequent tropism selection. Specifically, before and after packaging, they sequenced a random 7-mer peptide insertion library into AAV5, then used the data to train ML algorithms involving three linear additive models or four neural networks. The most predictive model (a neural network) was used to predict libraries that optimized both diversity and packaging efficiency, and subsequent experimental analysis of one such library showed superior packaging to the fully random library and a substantially greater number of variants that could infect primary human brain tissue slices58.

Combining functional selection, NGS, and ML-guided prediction has the potential to greatly accelerate AAV capsid engineering. These advances have allowed for the in silico design and subsequent experimental creation of massive libraries bridging ML and directed evolution,42,52,59 ML not only accelerates the biotechnology design process but also enhances our understanding of the underlying biology. These innovations thereby pave the way for more effective gene therapies.

## Conclusion

AAV vectors have emerged as a highly promising gene therapy platform that offer unmatched versatility in delivery to various tissues, relatively low immunogenicity, and the ability to transduce both dividing and non-dividing cells. However, the full realization of their therapeutic potential hinges on overcoming key challenges, including limited transduction efficiency, immune responses, tissue specificity, and manufacturing scalability.

This review has highlighted advances in AAV capsid engineering achieved through rational design, directed evolution, and ML-guided approaches. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain. Efficient crossing of biological hurdles such as the BBB, delivery to subjects positive for anti-AAV antibodies including during repeat dosing, mitigating immune responses to maximize safety, and achieving tissue specificity to enhance efficacy and safety still require progress. Furthermore, the underlying mechanisms of AAV transduction require a deeper understanding to optimize capsid functionality and minimize off-target effects. As the field progresses, the combination of expanded biological knowledge, innovative engineering strategies, and computational insights will pave the way for transformative AAV gene delivery vectors that can advance both scientific discovery and clinical outcomes.
